To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the X-ray spectrum of lobe-dominated broad-line AGN is hard (alpha(x) similar to -0.8) and that it is steeper than in core-dominated AGN (alpha(x) = -0.5).
the X-ray spectra of lobe-dominated, radio galaxies and quasars display a break at similar to 1-2-keV, with a steepening in the soft X-rays, and a hardening in the hard X-rays.

the hard X-ray emission in lobe-dominated, 2-Jy radio sources is produced by the same mechanism as in flat-spectrum/core dominated objects, namely by inverse Compton scattering of low-energy seed photons by relativistic electrons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the X-ray properties of a sample of lobe-dominated, flat-spectrum radio quasars, and the results are compared with those obtained for the same objects in the optical and radio bands.

the discovery of a hard, non-thermal X-ray component in the overall X-ray spectrum of lobe-dominated, 2-Jy broad-line radio galaxies and quasars, and with the demonstration that the same emission process is responsible for the hard X-ray emission in both lobe-dominated and core-dominated quasars.

the study of a class of sources which, although not as bright and powerful as flat-spectrum quasars, are nevertheless among the most luminous objects of the Universe and, as such, are of great importance to the understanding of the evolution of the universe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
all the objects of the sample have a two-component X-ray spectrum, with a hard power-law and a soft thermal component.
the X-ray emission from lobe-dominated, flat-spectrum radio sources is dominated by a nonthermal component with a flat spectrum.
the X-ray properties of lobe-dominated broad-line AGN are very similar to those of flat-spectrum quasars, but with the addition of a thermal component in the two broad line radio galaxies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the X-ray emission in these sources originates from two distinct components: one thermal and the other nonthermal.

lobe-dominated, flat-spectrum quasars and broad-line radio galaxies have very similar X-ray properties, with the only significant difference that the latter have a soft thermal component in addition to the hard power-law component.

the X-ray emission of lobe-dominated sources is dominated by two components: (1) an optically thick thermal component (most likely due to a hot plasma in the inner part of the accretion disk) and (2) a non-thermal, flat component (most likely inverse-Compton emission from the relativistic electrons in the jet).
The main takeaway from our work is that

lobe-dominated broad-line sources are characterized by hard X-ray spectra, with a break in their X-ray spectra at similar to 2 keV, which separates the soft (alpha(x) similar to or >1) from the hard X-ray (alpha(x) <1) emission.
lobe-dominated broad-line sources are not a homogeneous class of objects, but they include a variety of different X-ray properties.

lobe-dominated, flat-spectrum radio sources have similar X-ray properties as flat-spectrum/core- dominated objects, which suggests that both types of AGN are characterized by a common emission process, most likely inverse Compton scattering of relativistic electrons in the jet.
